stubs.angle: Asks what happens to an IDisposable object that is never disposed when it becomes unreachable and the garbage collector reclaims it.
stubs.answerHinge: The garbage collector never calls Dispose. It only reclaims memory, plus running a finalizer if the type has one, so unmanaged resources wait until finalization or leak.

stubs.angle: Asks which set of parts a compiled .NET assembly contains.
stubs.answerHinge: An assembly holds IL code, type metadata and a manifest that describes its identity, version and references. It does not hold native machine code for the JIT path.

stubs.angle: Shows two using declarations in one method whose Dispose methods print their names, and asks what the program prints.
stubs.answerHinge: Resources from using declarations are disposed at the end of the enclosing scope in reverse order of declaration, so the second resource is disposed first.

stubs.angle: Asks what the JIT compiler does and when a method's IL becomes native code.
stubs.answerHinge: The runtime compiles a method's IL to native code the first time the method is called. The result is reused for later calls in the same process, so the first call pays the compilation cost.

stubs.angle: Prints GC.GetGeneration of a still-referenced object after allocation and after each of two GC.Collect calls, and asks for the output.
stubs.answerHinge: A new small object starts in generation 0, and each collection it survives promotes it one generation up to generation 2, so the output is 0 1 2.

stubs.angle: Prints GC.GetGeneration for a fresh byte[84000] and a fresh byte[85000], and asks for the output.
stubs.answerHinge: Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the large object heap, which is collected with generation 2, so GC.GetGeneration reports 2 right after allocation. The smaller array starts in generation 0.

stubs.angle: Prints typeof(string).Assembly.GetName().Name on .NET 10 and asks for the output, with mscorlib and System.Runtime among the options.
stubs.answerHinge: In .NET (Core) the core types are implemented in System.Private.CoreLib. System.Runtime is only a reference facade and mscorlib belongs to .NET Framework, so the output is System.Private.CoreLib.

stubs.angle: A StreamWriter writes text into a MemoryStream without being disposed or flushed, then the code prints the stream length and gets 0, and the reader must find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: StreamWriter buffers its output and writes it to the underlying stream only on Flush or Dispose, so leaving out the using block leaves the data in the buffer.

stubs.angle: A short-lived subscriber attaches a handler to a static event and is never detached, and a WeakReference check after GC.Collect prints True instead of False.
stubs.answerHinge: The static event's delegate holds a strong reference to the subscriber, so the subscriber stays reachable from a static root until the handler is removed.

stubs.angle: Asks why a service that keeps allocating and freeing large arrays of different sizes can show LOH fragmentation, and which setting changes that.
stubs.answerHinge: By default the GC sweeps the large object heap but does not compact it. Compaction happens only on request, for example with GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode set to CompactOnce before a full blocking collection.

stubs.angle: Asks the reader to select every kind of reference that the garbage collector treats as a root.
stubs.answerHinge: Static fields, live local variables and parameters of executing methods, and strong GC handles are roots. A WeakReference target and an object referenced only by another unreachable object are not.

stubs.angle: A program creates an object whose finalizer prints a line, drops the reference and ends with a final print and no GC calls, and the question asks what .NET 10 prints.
stubs.answerHinge: Unlike .NET Framework, .NET (Core) does not run finalizers when the process exits, so only the final line is printed.

stubs.angle: A derived class overrides protected virtual Dispose(bool) to release its own resource but never calls the base implementation, so the program prints that the base resource is still open.
stubs.answerHinge: In the dispose pattern each override of Dispose(bool) must call base.Dispose(disposing), otherwise the resources owned by the base class are never released.

stubs.angle: Asks why an unreachable object with a finalizer is not reclaimed in the collection that finds it unreachable, and what this costs.
stubs.answerHinge: The GC moves an unreachable finalizable object to the f-reachable queue, which is a root, so the object and everything it references survive and are promoted. The memory is freed only by a later collection after the finalizer thread has run the finalizer.

stubs.angle: Asks how workstation and server GC differ and when you would choose each for a service running in a memory-limited container.
stubs.answerHinge: Server GC uses one heap and one GC thread per core for throughput, at the cost of larger memory use. Workstation GC uses a single heap with a smaller footprint, which suits small containers and client apps. Concurrent or background GC is a separate setting.

stubs.angle: A service's memory and gen 2 heap size grow for days until the container is OOM-killed, and the reader must say how to find the leak.
stubs.answerHinge: Confirm managed heap growth with dotnet-counters, take two dotnet-gcdump snapshots some time apart, compare which types grow and follow their paths to a root (static caches, event subscriptions, undisposed timers) before changing code.

stubs.angle: Asks the reader to select the true statements about tiered compilation, dynamic PGO and ReadyToRun code in .NET 8 and later.
stubs.answerHinge: Methods start with quick tier-0 code (or precompiled ReadyToRun code) and hot methods are recompiled at tier 1 using dynamic PGO, which is on by default since .NET 8. ReadyToRun code is therefore not final and can be replaced by the JIT.

stubs.angle: The team proposes publishing all backend services with Native AOT to cut startup time, and the reader must say how they would decide and roll it out.
stubs.answerHinge: Native AOT removes JIT startup cost and shrinks memory, but it forbids unbounded reflection and dynamic code loading, requires trim-safe dependencies and gives up dynamic PGO. Adopt it per service after checking trim and AOT warnings and measuring, not as a blanket rule.
